hero.headline: North Palm Beach celebrates Fourth of July with fireworks and America 250 events
hero.teaser: North Palm Beach residents and visitors will celebrate Independence Day with a full day of family-friendly activities, live entertainment and fireworks at North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse on July 4.
hero.body:
North Palm Beach is preparing a full day of Independence Day celebrations on July 4 at North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse. The free community event brings together family-friendly activities, live entertainment and fireworks to mark both the nation's birthday and America's 250th anniversary. Organizers emphasize that recognizing this milestone adds special meaning to the traditional holiday celebration in Palm Beach County.

The day begins at 11 a.m. with a community pool party at the country club pool area. Guests can take advantage of a water slide, enjoy DJ entertainment, and participate in various games and activities. The pool deck will feature food and beverages along with a poolside satellite bar. Event organizers note that the pool deck and lawn areas will create a festive atmosphere throughout the day's activities.

Starting at 4:30 p.m., families can engage in lawn games and activities such as cornhole, Connect 4, giant Jenga and face painting. The Clubhouse will serve a Fourth of July barbecue buffet beginning at the same time. Live music from the band Solstice Reign is scheduled to begin around 6 p.m., providing entertainment as the evening progresses.

The celebration culminates with a fireworks display at 9 p.m. Ashley Shipman, director of parks and recreation, highlighted that the golf course offers one of the best vantage points to view the fireworks. The combination of daytime pool activities, afternoon lawn games, evening dining and entertainment, and the nighttime fireworks finale creates a comprehensive celebration for North Palm Beach residents and visitors. The free admission to this community event makes it an accessible option for families throughout Palm Beach County looking to celebrate Independence Day together.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County residents face thousands in retroactive sewer fees from Delray Beach
cards.body:
Homeowners in an unincorporated Palm Beach County neighborhood are dealing with unexpected bills for years of unpaid sewer fees following a city audit. Residents along Franwood Drive received notices from the city of Delray Beach demanding back payments, with some bills exceeding $4,000. Candace Etzler received a notice for $3,139, while her neighbor Ruth Stephens was charged $4,494.92. At least a dozen homeowners in the area received similar notices covering up to three years of charges.

The retroactive billing stems from events in 1998, when nearby development disrupted the residents' septic systems. State law required them to connect to the nearest municipal sewer system. The city completed an audit in April 2026 that identified the sewer connections and triggered the back charges. Residents say they were caught off guard because they had previously attempted to pay but were told they did not need to. "We were in total shock because it feels like we're being punished," Stephens said. "We didn't make a mistake; we tried to pay, but they said we didn't have to."

The residents are questioning the calculation method for the back charges, which total $90 per month for 36 months. Etzler expressed frustration with the formula, asking "How can you have this random number of 36 months and at the price of $90 a month." Some homeowners have already paid the fees or enrolled in payment plans out of concern that their sewer service could be disconnected. "I understand having to pay a monthly fee, but my total was $4,494.92, and that's hard for people to just come up with," Stephens said.

City Commissioner Juli Casale defended the billing in a statement, explaining that when a sewer connection is identified, the city must determine what costs were incurred and recover applicable fees. "This is about ensuring that public utility costs are paid by those receiving the service rather than being shifted to the taxpayers," Casale said. County Commissioner Marci Woodward said she has contacted the county attorney to examine the legality of the back charges and the monthly payments going forward. The situation has left residents feeling unfairly treated for circumstances beyond their control.

cards.headline: Downtown West Palm Beach roads close Thursday for 4th on Flagler celebration
cards.teaser: Road closures begin at 4 p.m.
cards.body:
Drivers in downtown West Palm Beach should prepare for road closures beginning Thursday afternoon ahead of the annual 4th on Flagler celebration. Starting at 4 p.m. Thursday, July 2, several roads in the downtown area will close and remain closed through Sunday, July 5, according to the City of West Palm Beach.

The following road closures will be in effect: South Flagler Drive from Banyan Boulevard to Lakeview Avenue, the 100 blocks of Clematis Street, Datura Street and Evernia Street, the 200 blocks of Fern Street and Tanglewood Court, the 100 and 200 blocks of Trinity Place, Chase Avenue from Lakeview Avenue to South Flagler Drive, and Narcissus Avenue from Fern Street to Evernia Street. Drivers are encouraged to plan ahead, allow extra travel time and use alternate routes while the closures are in place. The annual 4th on Flagler celebration features live entertainment, family activities, food vendors and a fireworks display along the downtown waterfront. Residents can find additional information about traffic impacts and event details on the city's website.

cards.headline: Florida Manufactured Home Owners Can Now Apply for Storm Repair Funding Starting August 1
cards.teaser: A new Florida law that took effect Wednesday opens $167 million in state affordable housing funding to help mobile and manufactured home owners pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits.
cards.body:
Senate Bill 594, which took effect July 1, expands access to $167 million in state SHIP funding for manufactured home rent, emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits. The law passed in spring 2026 after an investigation exposed nearly 700,000 mobile and manufactured homes in Florida built before federal safety standards that cannot withstand modern storms. The investigation began after an EF-3 tornado destroyed homes in the Spanish Lakes Country Club Community of Fort Pierce, killing six residents and destroying 138 homes.

Julie Stellatos with Martin County Human Services said an online portal will open in August. About 75 percent of the county's annual SHIP funding, typically $1 million to $1.5 million, could now help eligible mobile and manufactured homeowners. Applicants can fill out an online application or call the office to request a mailed form. The funding operates on a first-come, first-served basis. Spanish Lakes resident Paula Richards said she does not have the $10,000 to $15,000 needed for storm-hardening repairs. Okeechobee County is updating its local housing assistance plan to offer lot rent, rehabilitation and emergency repair assistance once the program opens. St. Lucie County is waiting on final guidance from the state, while Indian River County plans to address the legislative change at a board meeting on August 18. The deadline for counties to submit plans to the state is September 30.

cards.headline: Martin County manufactured home owners can apply for storm repair funding starting in August
cards.body:
Martin County manufactured home owners will soon be able to apply for state funding to help with emergency repairs and storm-hardening improvements. An online application portal will open in August through Martin County Human Services. Once it launches, approximately 75 percent of the county's annual SHIP funding, which typically ranges from $1 million to $1.5 million, will become available to eligible mobile and manufactured homeowners.

This new program opportunity stems from Senate Bill 594, which took effect July 1st and expands access to $167 million in state affordable housing funding for manufactured home owners. The law makes money available for lot rent, emergency repairs, and storm-hardening retrofits. The legislative change was prompted by an investigation revealing that nearly 700,000 Florida mobile and manufactured homes, about two-thirds of the state's total housing stock, were built before current federal safety standards. These older homes cannot withstand modern storms, and many seniors living in them lack the financial resources to make necessary improvements. Repair estimates often range from $10,000 to $15,000 per home.

Julie Stellatos with Martin County Human Services says residents can complete applications online or request a paper version by calling the county office. Stellatos notes that homeowners have been requesting assistance long before this law passed. Since funding is distributed on a first-come, first-served basis, residents should prepare their documentation as soon as possible. Stellatos explains that all counties typically follow a similar timeline based on a calendar from the Florida Housing Coalition, though the specific schedule varies by county. Indian River County plans to present the legislative changes to its Board on August 18th with a state submission deadline of September 30th. St. Lucie County is still awaiting final state guidance before announcing its application process, while Okeechobee County is updating its local housing assistance plan to comply with the new law.

Residents can begin preparing now by visiting the Florida Housing Finance Corporation website and selecting their county or city. The website provides information about available funding, income eligibility requirements, contact information, and application instructions. Gathering necessary paperwork ahead of the portal opening will help ensure applicants can submit their requests quickly when the system becomes active.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach gets $2 million in state funding for Australian Avenue flood repairs
cards.teaser: Storm-weary drivers and residents along Australian Avenue could see relief after years of flooding with every rain. The new Florida budget includes $2 million for drainage improvements from Banyan Boulevard through 45th Street.
cards.body:
The new Florida budget signed Monday by Gov. Ron DeSantis includes $2 million in state funding for a drainage project along Australian Avenue in West Palm Beach, targeting the stretch from Banyan Boulevard through 45th Street. State Sen. Mack Bernard called the funding a major step forward after the governor vetoed $742,000 for the project last June. The $2 million represents only a portion of the project's estimated $65 million cost, but residents say it is progress they have waited years to see.

For many residents, flooding along the roadway is not limited to major storms. Theodore Vanriel, who lives near the corridor, said even light rain causes streets to flood and that he has been riding his bike through flooded streets since childhood. Marion Hawkins, who lives near the roadway, said water comes all the way up to her driveway and yard, leaving debris scattered across her property. She calls it "Lake Australian Avenue." Palm Beach County Public Works Director and Engineer David Ricks presented improvement plans three years ago that included creating a larger median and expanding road and shoulder areas to accommodate larger underground drainage pipes. According to Palm Beach County documents, the Australian Avenue improvements are part of a five-year road program scheduled through 2029.

cards.headline: Palm Beach International Airport signage changes underway for Trump name
cards.teaser: Palm Beach International Airport is becoming Donald J. Trump International Airport, with the official name change set to take effect July 9. Signs are already being swapped out as part of a transition funded by the state at $2.75 million.
cards.body:
Palm Beach International Airport is transitioning to Donald J. Trump International Airport, with the official name change set to take effect July 9. The airport remains owned by Palm Beach County, but Trump owns the trademark on the new name. The three-letter designation will change from PBI to DJT for airline reservations and navigation purposes in August. Sign changes are happening gradually and are being funded by the state of Florida at a cost of $2.75 million. Airport officials said nothing should change for passengers beyond the signage.

The airport posted a statement on its website acknowledging that "the required name change may be received in different ways by our passengers." Travelers have expressed mixed reactions to the change. Two lawsuits are attempting to stop the name change. George Poncy, one of the plaintiffs suing to block it, said the state appears to be stalling and delaying any hearing before a judge. Sign changes will happen gradually, with passengers likely among the first to notice the transition as it unfolds.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz closed after one year of operation amid lawsuits and questions
cards.teaser: One year after Florida opened an immigration detention facility in the Everglades called Alligator Alcatraz, the facility has closed. The state project cost more than $1 billion, and questions remain about whether Florida taxpayers will be reimbursed.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump announced the opening of Alligator Alcatraz alongside Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis on July 1, 2025, describing it as a place to house what he called the most dangerous migrants in the country. The state used emergency powers to commandeer an old landing strip belonging to Miami-Dade County, then used emergency funding and no-bid contracts through the Florida Division of Emergency Management to build the facility in eight days. Trump said the Federal Emergency Management Agency would pay for the facility.

Using ICE's own data, investigators uncovered that about 70 percent of detainees there had no criminal record. Immigration attorneys and detainees raised alarms about conditions inside. A district court judge in August sided with environmental groups including Friends of the Everglades, led by Director Eve Samples, issuing a preliminary injunction that ordered the state and federal governments to dismantle Alligator Alcatraz. An appeals court reversed that decision in September. A $608 million FEMA grant approved in October was stalled, leaving Florida taxpayers to cover costs estimated at more than $1 billion. On June 16, ICE confirmed that all detainees had been removed in preparation for hurricane season. DeSantis said 21,000 detainees were deported through the facility. The ACLU and Friends of the Everglades lawsuits remain active.

cards.headline: Jensen Beach teen Harper Aberman to represent Team USA at Sailing World Championship in France
cards.teaser: Harper Aberman of Jensen Beach will represent Team USA at the Sailing World Championship in France this weekend. The teenager began her competitive sailing career at the US Sailing Center of Martin County.
cards.body:
Harper Aberman, a Jensen Beach teenager, will represent Team USA at the Sailing World Championship in France this weekend. Aberman started sailing at age four at a four-week summer camp in Pennsylvania that her grandparents enrolled her in. After her family moved to Jensen Beach, she joined the green fleet program at the US Sailing Center of Martin County, where her competitive career took shape.

Aberman describes herself as an adrenaline junkie and says the sport's most challenging conditions draw her in. She has won countless tournaments, placed in several national competitions, and is considered one of the biggest names in the youth sailing circuit. Aberman learned she would represent Team USA during Spring Break. She has spent the past few weeks training in Spain ahead of the competition, with racing set to begin Monday.

cards.headline: Benjamin Franklin artifact collection to go on display at Historical Society of Palm Beach County
cards.teaser: One of the largest collections of Benjamin Franklin artifacts will be on display at the Historical Society of Palm Beach County in downtown West Palm Beach starting July 6. The exhibit is free to the public and runs through August 31.
cards.body:
Zachary Jacobson of Palm Beach Gardens owns one of the largest Benjamin Franklin artifact collections, which he shares with his brother. The brothers are displaying the collection to celebrate America's 250th birthday through an exhibit titled Benjamin Franklin: Creating an American Icon at the Historical Society of Palm Beach County in downtown West Palm Beach. The exhibit features over 50 books written by, printed by or about Franklin, along with work from his time as a printer. Artwork of the founding father covers the walls, including an original portrait.

Among the standout pieces is a grandfather clock originally from Franklin's home in Philadelphia, a plate inscribed "B. Franklin," and original medallions made when Franklin was representing France during the American Revolution. Additional highlights include a copy of Experiments and Observations on Electricity Made at Philadelphia owned by Franklin's son William, a tall-case tidal clock kept in Franklin's Philadelphia home, and a plaster model for the Libertas Americana medal designed by Franklin and executed by Augustin Dupre. Jacobson's stepfather started the collection 50 years ago. Jacobson and his brother eventually bought the remains and continued it for 15 years. More than 120 pieces are on display. The free exhibit opens July 6 and runs through August at 300 N Dixie Hwy.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach woman raises funds for best friend's family after Venezuela earthquakes kill relatives
cards.teaser: Alessandra De La Correa spent six agonizing hours wondering whether her parents were alive after two devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira, collapsing buildings and killing members of her family.
cards.body:
Two devastating earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira last week, collapsing buildings and killing several members of Alessandra De La Correa's family. Her parents survived, but she lost her 17-year-old cousin Claudia, her grandmother, her uncle and his wife. De La Correa's best friend since high school, Carla Alvarado, who now lives in West Palm Beach, woke De La Correa with nonstop phone calls in the middle of the night after the earthquakes struck. The losses came just weeks after De La Correa returned from her first visit to Venezuela in several years to announce she and her partner are expecting a baby later this year. During her final weekend in the country, the family gathered together for Mother's Day.

Claudia, a volleyball player who had planned to study dentistry, had been rehearsing a dance routine with classmates when the building collapsed. De La Correa's uncle, a former Navy member, searched through the rubble in darkness after the quake knocked out electricity across the area. When he found Claudia dead beneath the debris, he stayed behind to help rescue her trapped best friend for around 13 hours, but the girl was killed after another section of the structure collapsed during rescue efforts. The earthquakes also destroyed De La Correa's parents' home and her mother's children's clothing store, which was located inside a shopping mall that collapsed entirely. Alvarado launched a GoFundMe campaign aiming to raise $15,000 to support De La Correa's relatives.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce man arrested on drug trafficking charges after meth and MDMA seized
cards.teaser: A Fort Pierce man faces drug trafficking charges after deputies found methamphetamine and MDMA during a search.
cards.body:
Deputies arrested a Fort Pierce man on drug trafficking charges after discovering methamphetamine and MDMA during a search. The arrest occurred Wednesday as part of an investigation by local law enforcement.

Authorities seized quantities of both controlled substances during the operation. The man now faces multiple drug trafficking charges related to the seized narcotics. Deputies completed the search and booking on Wednesday.

cards.headline: Man arrested after driving truck into Indian River County convenience store
cards.teaser: A man was arrested Wednesday after driving a truck into a convenience store in Indian River County.
cards.body:
A driver crashed a truck into a convenience store in Indian River County on Wednesday, leading to an arrest. The incident occurred at a local convenience store when the vehicle drove into the building.

Deputies responded to the scene and arrested the driver following the crash. The man was taken into custody after the collision with the store. Authorities completed the arrest Wednesday evening.

cards.headline: Dave & Buster's employee stops suspected impaired driver in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: A Dave & Buster's employee in Port St. Lucie is being praised for stopping a suspected impaired driver.
cards.body:
An employee at Dave & Buster's in Port St. Lucie intervened to stop a suspected impaired driver, earning praise from local authorities. The employee took action when they observed signs of impairment in a customer attempting to drive.

The incident occurred recently at the Port St. Lucie location of the entertainment venue. The employee's quick thinking prevented the suspected impaired person from getting behind the wheel. Local law enforcement commended the employee for their vigilance and community safety awareness.

cards.headline: St. Lucie scanner Facebook page distances itself from founder after Orbeez arrest
cards.teaser: A St. Lucie County scanner Facebook page has distanced itself from its founder following an arrest related to Orbeez.
cards.body:
A popular St. Lucie County police scanner Facebook page has publicly separated from its founder after the person was arrested in connection with an Orbeez incident. The page administrators announced the decision to distance themselves from the founder following the arrest.

The founder faced charges related to Orbeez, the small gel beads that expand in water. The arrest prompted the page's current operators to make clear they are no longer affiliated with the original founder. The Facebook page continues to operate under new management separate from the arrested individual.

hero.headline: Martin County clinic sees surge in patients after federal health subsidies expire
hero.teaser: Volunteers in Medicine in Martin County is treating more uninsured patients after enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies ended in January, leaving more than 200,000 Floridians without coverage.
hero.body:
Volunteers in Medicine, a free clinic serving low-income families in Martin County, is experiencing increased patient demand following the expiration of enhanced federal subsidies under the Affordable Care Act at the beginning of this year. Dr. Jordan Bromberg, the clinic's medical director, reports that more than 200,000 people across Florida chose not to renew their health insurance through the ACA program. While the clinic has directly served about 20 patients who lost coverage, Bromberg estimates that upwards of 500 Martin County residents may have lost access to health insurance entirely.

The loss of subsidies has created a difficult situation for families already struggling financially. Rokaya McGarry, one of the clinic's recent patients, found herself unable to maintain health insurance after the enhanced assistance program ended. Without coverage, McGarry initially viewed medical care as a luxury she could no longer afford. This perspective changed when she fell seriously ill following her mother's death. "The grief and the everything I had like a bronchitis I felt very weak and in a moment of desperation," McGarry said. "I called and within a day VIM clinic took over." McGarry expressed her relief at receiving care, saying "I can't even express how grateful I am to them because I don't know where I'd be."

The expiration of the enhanced subsidies has removed critical financial protection for vulnerable populations. According to Bromberg, early medical screening can identify conditions before they develop into serious health problems. "There are a lot of things that get screened for that if they're found early can prevent terrible outcomes," he noted. The clinic's ability to catch medical issues at early stages becomes even more important when patients have no other access to healthcare.

Volunteers in Medicine maintains eligibility requirements to serve those most in need. Individuals earning under $39,990 annually or families of four earning under $82,500 per year qualify for the clinic's services. Despite the increase in patient volume, Bromberg indicated the clinic has capacity to serve additional patients from the community. "There are so many more out there that can come and see us," he said. "We have the capacity for more." The clinic continues offering comprehensive medical care at no cost and without conditions attached to those who qualify for assistance.

Aberman started sailing at age four when her grandparents enrolled her in a four-week summer camp in Pennsylvania. After completing the initial four-week course, she returned for eight weeks. "That is where the sailing adventure took off for me," Aberman said after her family moved to Jensen Beach and she joined the green fleet program at the US Sailing Center of Martin County.

Aberman describes herself as an adrenaline junkie and says the sport's most challenging conditions draw her in. She has won countless tournaments, placed in several national competitions, and is considered one of the biggest names in the youth sailing circuit. Aberman received news of her selection during Spring Break via email. "It was during Spring Break, I got the email. I started screaming, my parents started screaming, and we were like, 'This is not real. We're going to Europe this summer," she said. She has spent the past few weeks training in Spain ahead of the competition, which begins Monday.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach receives $2 million state funding for Australian Avenue flood repairs
cards.teaser: Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a budget that includes $2 million for drainage improvements along Australian Avenue from Banyan Boulevard through 45th Street, an area that floods during routine rain.
cards.body:
The Florida budget signed Monday by Gov. Ron DeSantis includes $2 million in state funding for a drainage project along Australian Avenue in West Palm Beach. The project targets Australian Avenue from Banyan Boulevard through 45th Street, an area Palm Beach County leaders have identified as needing major drainage improvements. State Sen. Mack Bernard secured the funding after DeSantis vetoed $742,000 for the project last June.

Residents say the area floods during even light storms. Theodore Vanriel, who lives near the corridor, said he has been riding his bike through flooded streets since he was a child. Marion Hawkins, who lives near the roadway, calls it Lake Australian Avenue, noting that rainwater comes all the way up to her driveway and yard and leaves debris. The $2 million covers only a portion of the project's estimated $65 million cost. Palm Beach County Public Works Director and Engineer David Ricks presented plans three years ago that included creating a larger median and expanding road and shoulder areas to make room for larger underground drainage pipes designed to reduce flooding. According to Palm Beach County documents, the Australian Avenue improvements are part of a five-year road program scheduled to run through 2029.

cards.headline: Florida manufactured home owners can apply for repair funding starting in August
cards.teaser: Nearly 140 new Florida laws took effect Wednesday, including Senate Bill 594 that opens $167 million in state funding to help mobile and manufactured home owners pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits.
cards.body:
Senate Bill 594 took effect July 1st and opens up $167 million in state affordable housing funding to help mobile and manufactured home owners pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits. The law follows an investigation that found nearly 700,000 mobile and manufactured homes in Florida, about two-thirds of the state's more than 1 million such homes, were built before today's federal safety standards. The investigation started after an EF-3 tornado destroyed 138 homes and killed six people at Spanish Lakes Country Club Community of Fort Pierce.

Julie Stellatos with Martin County Human Services said an online portal will open in August. About 75% of the county's annual SHIP funding, typically $1 million to $1.5 million, could now help eligible mobile and manufactured homeowners. Applicants can fill out an online application or call the office to have one mailed. Okeechobee County is updating its local housing assistance plan to comply with the new law and plans to offer lot rent, rehabilitation and emergency repair assistance once the program opens. St. Lucie County is waiting on final guidance from the state before announcing its application process. Indian River County staff are taking an item regarding the legislative change to the Board on August 18, with a September 30 deadline to submit their plan to the state. Stellatos said the process is first come, first served, so applicants should gather paperwork quickly.

cards.headline: Benjamin Franklin artifact collection opens July 6 at Historical Society of Palm Beach County
cards.teaser: One of the largest collections of Benjamin Franklin artifacts will go on display at the Historical Society of Palm Beach County in downtown West Palm Beach starting July 6, featuring over 120 pieces from the collection of Zachary Jacobson of Palm Beach Gardens.
cards.body:
Benjamin Franklin: Creating an American Icon opens July 6 at the Historical Society of Palm Beach County, located at 300 N Dixie Hwy in downtown West Palm Beach. Zachary Jacobson of Palm Beach Gardens owns the collection with his brother and is displaying it to celebrate America's 250th birthday. The exhibit, free to the public, runs through August and features more than 120 pieces covering Franklin's roles as statesman, printer and inventor.

The exhibit includes over 50 books written by, printed by or about Franklin, along with work from his time as a printer. Artwork of the founding father covers the walls, including an original portrait. Standout pieces include a grandfather clock originally from Franklin's home in Philadelphia, a plate inscribed "B. Franklin," original medallions made when Franklin was representing France during the American Revolution, and the glass armonica, which Franklin called his favorite invention. Jacobson's stepfather started the collection 50 years ago. Jacobson and his brother eventually bought the collection and continued it for 15 years.

cards.headline: Vacant Wellington Nordstrom could become 620-unit apartment complex
cards.teaser: Bainbridge Companies submitted plans to convert 18 acres of the empty Nordstrom store at the Mall at Wellington Green into a 620-unit multifamily apartment complex that would include three towers and a parking structure.
cards.body:
Bainbridge Companies submitted plans to the village of Wellington to transform the vacant Nordstrom at the Mall at Wellington Green into a 620-unit multifamily apartment complex on 18 acres. The existing building would be demolished if the project is approved. Village Manager Jim Barnes said the development would include one-, two- and three-bedroom units, three towers and a parking structure.

Barnes said the project addresses a broader housing shortage throughout the county, state and beyond. Some residents oppose the proposal. Richard Meyers, who has lived in Wellington for more than a decade, said there are already apartment complexes around the mall and he does not think more are needed. Other residents raised concerns about traffic impact, with Gaby Martinez saying the added density could strain local roads and create bottlenecks during daily commutes. Barnes suggested new development nearby could benefit the retailers that remain at the mall, noting that Macy's, Dillard's and JCPenney are high-performing stores. He said the Macy's at the Mall at Wellington Green is the highest-performing store in the state. No timeline or cost estimate for the project has been announced and the plans have not been approved.

hero.headline: Martin County Free Clinic Has Capacity for More Patients After ACA Subsidies Expired
hero.teaser: Volunteers in Medicine clinic in Martin County is treating more patients who lost health insurance when enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies expired in January. The clinic says it can serve additional uninsured residents.
hero.body:
Volunteers in Medicine, a free medical clinic serving low-income families in Martin County, is experiencing increased demand following the expiration of enhanced financial assistance through the Affordable Care Act at the beginning of 2026. According to Dr. Jordan Bromberg, the clinic's medical director, more than 200,000 people statewide in Florida did not renew their health insurance through the ACA this year. He estimates that upwards of 500 Martin County residents lost access to coverage as a result of the subsidy expiration.

Despite the growing need, the clinic has treated only about 20 patients who specifically lost ACA coverage so far. Bromberg emphasizes that the clinic maintains sufficient capacity to serve significantly more uninsured patients. One of those patients is Rokaya McGarry, a Martin County resident whose inability to afford health insurance after the subsidies ended forced her to seek care at the clinic. When she fell seriously ill with bronchitis following her mother's death, she called the clinic in desperation and received medical attention within a day.

Bromberg underscores the importance of early health screening in preventing serious medical complications. He notes that many health conditions can be identified during preventive care visits, allowing for interventions that prevent worse outcomes down the line. For individuals without insurance, the clinic provides an essential safety net that helps them avoid waiting until conditions become severe enough to require emergency room treatment.

To qualify for free care at Volunteers in Medicine, individuals must have annual earnings below $39,990, or families of four must earn under $82,500 per year. The clinic offers medical services with no additional requirements or strings attached. McGarry expressed profound gratitude for the clinic's support, saying she does not know where she would have turned otherwise. With hundreds of Martin County residents estimated to have lost insurance coverage and the clinic equipped to handle more patients, Bromberg encourages eligible uninsured residents to access the care available to them.

cards.headline: Jensen Beach Teen Harper Aberman to Represent Team USA at Sailing World Championship in France
cards.teaser: Harper Aberman, a Jensen Beach teenager, will represent Team USA at the Sailing World Championship in France beginning Monday after years of competitive sailing.
cards.body:
Harper Aberman, a Jensen Beach teenager, will represent Team USA at the Sailing World Championship in France this weekend after years of competitive sailing that began at age four. Aberman first fell in love with sailing at a four-week summer camp in Pennsylvania where her grandparents enrolled her and her cousin. While her cousin disliked the experience, Aberman stayed for eight weeks and continued sailing after her family moved to Jensen Beach.

Aberman joined the green fleet program at the US Sailing Center of Martin County, where her competitive career took shape. She describes herself as an adrenaline junkie drawn to the sport's most challenging conditions. Despite struggling to stay upright in windy weather, Aberman has won countless tournaments, placed in several national competitions, and is considered one of the biggest names in the youth sailing circuit. She received notification of her Team USA selection via email during Spring Break, prompting her and her parents to scream in disbelief at the news. Aberman has spent the past few weeks training in Spain ahead of the competition, with racing set to begin Monday.

cards.headline: Florida Manufactured Home Owners Can Now Apply for Storm Repair Funding Starting August 1
cards.teaser: A new Florida law that took effect Wednesday opens $167 million in state affordable housing funding to help mobile and manufactured home owners pay for emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits.
cards.body:
Senate Bill 594, which took effect July 1, expands access to $167 million in state SHIP funding for manufactured home rent, emergency repairs and storm-hardening retrofits. The law passed in spring 2026 after an investigation exposed nearly 700,000 mobile and manufactured homes in Florida built before federal safety standards that cannot withstand modern storms. The investigation began after an EF-3 tornado destroyed homes in the Spanish Lakes Country Club Community of Fort Pierce, killing six residents and destroying 138 homes.

Julie Stellatos with Martin County Human Services said an online portal will open in August. About 75 percent of the county's annual SHIP funding, typically $1 million to $1.5 million, could now help eligible mobile and manufactured homeowners. Applicants can fill out an online application or call the office to request a mailed form. The funding operates on a first-come, first-served basis. Spanish Lakes resident Paula Richards said she does not have the $10,000 to $15,000 needed for storm-hardening repairs. Okeechobee County is updating its local housing assistance plan to offer lot rent, rehabilitation and emergency repair assistance once the program opens. St. Lucie County is waiting on final guidance from the state, while Indian River County plans to address the legislative change at a board meeting on August 18. The deadline for counties to submit plans to the state is September 30.

cards.headline: Vacant Nordstrom at Mall at Wellington Green Could Become 620-Unit Apartment Complex
cards.teaser: Bainbridge Companies submitted plans to convert 18 acres of the empty Nordstrom store at the Mall at Wellington Green into a 620-unit multifamily apartment complex that would demolish the existing building.
cards.body:
Bainbridge Companies submitted plans to Wellington village officials to convert the vacant Nordstrom at the Mall at Wellington Green into a 620-unit multifamily apartment complex spanning 18 acres. The development would include one-, two- and three-bedroom units featuring three towers and a parking structure, according to Village Manager Jim Barnes. The existing Nordstrom building would be demolished if the project receives approval.

Barnes said the project addresses a housing shortage throughout the county and state. He noted that additional development near the mall could benefit remaining retailers, including Macy's, Dillard's and JCPenney, which continue to perform well. Barnes said the Macy's at the Mall at Wellington Green is the highest-performing store in the state. Some residents oppose the proposal. Richard Meyers, who has lived in Wellington for more than a decade, said the area already has multiple apartment complexes and does not need more. Gaby Martinez raised concerns about traffic impacts, saying the added density could create bottlenecks on local roads. The village has not announced a timeline or cost estimate for the project, and the plans have not been approved.

cards.headline: Delray Beach to Open 1976 Bicentennial Time Capsule During Fourth of July Celebration
cards.teaser: Delray Beach will open a time capsule from the 1976 Bicentennial on the main stage during its annual Fourth of July celebration on Saturday, which expects to draw more than 20,000 people.
cards.body:
The City of Delray Beach will open a 1976 Bicentennial time capsule on the main stage at Atlantic Avenue and A1A during its annual Fourth of July celebration on Saturday. The event, a family tradition for over 50 years, typically draws more than 20,000 people. The time capsule opening is scheduled for 5:30 p.m. on the main stage, followed by a 60-foot flag raising with the National Anthem at 6 p.m. at Atlantic Avenue and Seabreeze Avenue.

The celebration begins at 5 p.m., with additional daytime activities starting at 8 a.m. Live music and entertainment will take place on multiple stages, with non-stop performances by Digital Vibez. All-day activities include food trucks, vendors, arts and crafts, face painting, glitter tattoos, carnival games, a photo booth and toddler soft play. The 4's on the 4th Volleyball Tournament runs from 8 a.m. to noon at the south end of the municipal beach, and a sand sculpting contest sponsored by Delray Beach Rotary and Kiwanis Clubs will also be held. Snorkeling and scuba dive tours of the S.S. Inchulva "Delray Wreck" are available from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. Fireworks conclude the evening. The public is urged to park west of the Intracoastal Bridge, with free rides available through the FreeBee app in the downtown area.

cards.headline: Boca Raton Hosts Full Day of Events Saturday to Mark America's 250th Birthday
cards.teaser: Boca Raton's 68-year-old Independence Day tradition returns with events from a sunrise 5K to evening fireworks as the city celebrates America's 250th anniversary on Saturday.
cards.body:
Boca Raton will celebrate America's 250th birthday on Saturday, July 4, 2026, with a full day of events across multiple locations. The Firecracker 5K begins at 7:15 a.m. at Florida Atlantic University at 777 Glades Road, with $40 registration required in advance and no on-site registration available. The Liberty Cup Pickleball and Tennis Tournament starts at 8 a.m., with pickleball at Patch Reef Park and tennis at The Racquet Center. From 1 to 4 p.m., the Fabulous Fourth Block Party runs at Sugar Sand Park at 300 South Military Trail, offering free admission with kids' crafts, yard games, a DJ and food trucks.

The Fabulous Finale takes place from 6:30 to 9:30 p.m. at Countess de Hoernle Park at 1000 Spanish River Boulevard, featuring free admission with live music at 6:30 p.m. and 7:30 p.m. and a 20-minute fireworks display at 9:10 p.m. Free parking is available at Boca Raton Innovation Campus with entry from Yamato Road, and ride-share drop-off is at 4530 Technology Way. Free trolley service runs from 6:30 p.m. through the event's end, though strollers must be fully collapsed to board. A1A will be closed at the Deerfield and Boca border from 7 p.m. until Deerfield Beach fireworks conclude. No pets, coolers, sparklers, drones, alcohol or glass bottles are permitted, and free filtered water is available on-site.

cards.headline: Lake Worth Beach to Feature First-Ever Drone Show During Fourth of July Celebration
cards.teaser: Lake Worth Beach will debut a 300-drone light show during its Fourth of July celebration at Bryant Park on Saturday, along with a skydiving performance and concerts.
cards.body:
The City of Lake Worth Beach will celebrate America's 250th anniversary with its first-ever drone light show on Saturday, July 4, 2026, at Bryant Park. The 15-minute drone show featuring 300 drones is scheduled for 8:45 p.m. and will be best viewed from Bryant Park facing southwest. A six-minute fireworks display with more than 11,700 shots will follow at 9 p.m. The event is free and expected to draw 10,000 people.

The celebration includes additional entertainment and activities throughout the day. The Great American Raft Race, hosted by the Neighborhood Association Presidents' Council, begins at noon. A hot dog eating contest with six contestants is scheduled for 5:30 p.m. Concert performances start at 7 p.m. with Sekond Nature, followed by Elton and the Jets, an Elton John tribute band, at 8:30 and 9:30 p.m. A skydiving performance by the All Veteran Group is scheduled for 7:45 p.m., including a tandem jump by Vice Mayor Mimi May carrying a special American flag commemorating the nation's 250th anniversary. The Lake Worth Beach Bridge will be closed to vehicles and pedestrians from 8 to 10 p.m. Ride-share drop-off is available at Fourth Avenue South and South Lakeside Drive at South Bryant Park.

hero.headline: North Palm Beach celebrates Fourth of July with fireworks and America 250 events
hero.teaser: North Palm Beach residents and visitors will celebrate Independence Day with a full day of family-friendly activities, live entertainment and fireworks at North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse on July 4.
hero.body:
North Palm Beach is preparing a full day of Independence Day celebrations on July 4 at North Palm Beach Country Club and The Clubhouse. The free community event brings together family-friendly activities, live entertainment and fireworks to mark both the nation's birthday and America's 250th anniversary. Organizers emphasize that recognizing this milestone adds special meaning to the traditional holiday celebration in Palm Beach County.

The day begins at 11 a.m. with a community pool party at the country club pool area. Guests can take advantage of a water slide, enjoy DJ entertainment, and participate in various games and activities. The pool deck will feature food and beverages along with a poolside satellite bar. Event organizers note that the pool deck and lawn areas will create a festive atmosphere throughout the day's activities.

Starting at 4:30 p.m., families can engage in lawn games and activities such as cornhole, Connect 4, giant Jenga and face painting. The Clubhouse will serve a Fourth of July barbecue buffet beginning at the same time. Live music from the band Solstice Reign is scheduled to begin around 6 p.m., providing entertainment as the evening progresses.

The celebration culminates with a fireworks display at 9 p.m. Ashley Shipman, director of parks and recreation, highlighted that the golf course offers one of the best vantage points to view the fireworks. The combination of daytime pool activities, afternoon lawn games, evening dining and entertainment, and the nighttime fireworks finale creates a comprehensive celebration for North Palm Beach residents and visitors. The free admission to this community event makes it an accessible option for families throughout Palm Beach County looking to celebrate Independence Day together.

cards.headline: Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach offers sea turtle programs through September
cards.teaser: Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach is offering a variety of educational and interactive programs during peak sea turtle nesting season this summer.
cards.body:
Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach is offering educational and interactive programs during peak sea turtle nesting season through September. Guests can participate in guided Turtle Walks, the Hatchling Discovery Program, Hatchling Releases, Tidal Tots and Plastic Free July Community Action Day. The center's Turtle Walk program allows participants to observe the nesting process while learning about sea turtle biology, conservation and ongoing research efforts. Educational demonstrations may include the use of red-light headlamps, amber lighting, night scopes and research tag scanning equipment.

The programs are designed to give visitors an opportunity to learn more about sea turtle conservation along one of the world's busiest sea turtle nesting beaches. Loggerhead Marinelife Center's education and research departments work together during nesting season to collect and analyze data related to nesting activity and hatchling success. Sea turtle nesting season in Florida typically runs from March through October. Conservation groups continue encouraging beachgoers to turn off beachfront lighting at night, properly dispose of trash and avoid disturbing nesting turtles or hatchlings. Registration information and program details are available through Loggerhead Marinelife Center.

hero.headline: Florida CFO Blaise Ingoglia endorses Byron Donalds for Governor, consolidating GOP establishment support
hero.body:
Florida Chief Financial Officer Blaise Ingoglia has endorsed Byron Donalds for Governor, marking another significant addition to what has become a roster of top Republican establishment figures backing the Trump-endorsed candidate. Ingoglia and Donalds served together in the Florida House, a shared legislative history that informed his decision to support the gubernatorial bid. Ingoglia praised Donalds' conservative record during his time in both the state House and Congress, and highlighted his private sector experience as preparation for addressing two major issues facing Florida residents: affordability and the state's insurance market challenges. In a statement, Ingoglia said Donalds will defend conservative achievements and defeat what he called the radical Democrats threatening Florida's future.

Donalds acknowledged the endorsement by referencing their time together in the state legislature. He expressed gratitude for Ingoglia's support and positioned the endorsement as part of a broader effort to advance his vision for Florida's economy and freedoms. Donalds stated that Florida's best days remain ahead and emphasized his commitment to building an economy that serves families while protecting the state's exceptional character through conservative leadership.

Ingoglia joins a growing list of Republican power players already backing Donalds. Attorney General James Uthmeier, incoming House Speaker Sam Garrison, and Senate President-designate Jim Boyd have all endorsed the candidate. This consolidation of establishment support reflects a broader wave of conservative leadership uniting behind Donalds well before the primary election takes place. The alignment of major officeholders behind a single candidate in a competitive race demonstrates the extent to which establishment Republicans have coalesced around his campaign.

Donalds' fundraising has paralleled this political momentum. He posted a record $22 million in his opening quarter, a financial advantage that has created significant obstacles for potential rivals considering a challenge. The combination of Trump's endorsement, backing from sitting statewide officials, and substantial campaign resources has positioned Donalds as the frontrunner in Florida's Republican gubernatorial race months before voters go to the polls.

cards.headline: Democratic challenger Leela Gray raises over $1 million to unseat Rep. Anna Paulina Luna in Florida's 13th District
cards.teaser: Retired Brigadier General Leela Gray passed the seven-figure fundraising milestone in five months, with 90% from small contributions under $100.
cards.body:
Democratic congressional candidate Leela Gray has raised more than $1 million since launching her campaign to challenge Republican U.S. Rep. Anna Paulina Luna in Florida's 13th Congressional District. The Pinellas Democrat reached the seven-figure milestone five months after launching her campaign. Gray's campaign reported that 90% of donations came from small contributions of less than $100. The retired Brigadier General closed the second quarter with $750,000 in cash on hand.

Gray is running to unseat Luna, a Pinellas Republican first elected in 2022 when she flipped a seat previously held by a Democrat. Gray has attracted endorsements from several sitting members of Congress, including Democratic U.S. Reps. Kathy Castor of Tampa, Lois Frankel of West Palm Beach, Jason Crow of Colorado, Ted Lieu of California and Pat Ryan of New York. Former Chief Financial Officer Alex Sink, former state Rep. Ben Diamond and Safety Harbour Mayor Joe Ayoub have also endorsed her campaign. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee lists CD 13 among GOP-held Districts in Play for this year's Midterms. Before facing Luna, Gray must first win the Democratic Primary against intelligence analyst John Liccione and educator Brandt Robinson on August 1.

cards.headline: Floridians on Medicare forced to skip doses as prescription drug costs surge
cards.teaser: Medicare patients report cholesterol medication costs jumping from $140 to $572, forcing patients to cut pills or skip doses to stretch supplies.
cards.body:
Floridians on Medicare are struggling with skyrocketing prescription drug costs that force difficult choices. Judith Waska, a Medicare recipient, said her cholesterol medication cost around $140 for three months before jumping to $572 with the deductible. She pointed out that patients on commercial insurance could obtain the same medication for $25 using a coupon, calling the disparity unfair. A 2023 study by Health Care Value Hub found more than a quarter of Floridians are cutting pills or skipping doses to make their medications last longer.

Dr. Shawn Baca with Rheumatology Associates of South Florida said he sees the cost barrier every day in his practice. He explained that insurance companies charge patients co-pays based on the list price rather than the discounted price. Baca compared medication cost changes to buying a car, noting that prices may shift year to year as formulas change. Karen Harwood, executive director of community programs for the Palm Beach County Medical Society, advised patients to visit the Social Security Office to determine financial eligibility for supplemental programs, which offer different levels and percentages of assistance. Experts also recommended that patients speak with their doctor or insurance company about lower cost medication alternatives.

cards.headline: American pride hits record low at 33% ahead of 250th Independence Day anniversary
cards.teaser: Only 33% of Americans say they are extremely proud to be American, the lowest figure in Gallup polling dating back to 2001.
cards.body:
American pride has hit a record low as the nation approaches its 250th birthday. According to Gallup's latest survey, only 33% of Americans say they are "extremely proud" to be American, marking the lowest figure in polling on the issue dating back to 2001. An additional 20% say they are "very proud," while 22% are "moderately proud," 15% are "only a little proud," and 9% are "not at all proud."

The decline represents a dramatic shift from earlier decades. When Gallup first asked this question in 2001, 55% of U.S. adults were extremely proud to be American. Pride surged after 9/11, with 65% to 70% of Americans expressing extreme pride through 2004. Extreme pride held at majority levels through 2017 but has declined sharply since 2018, when no more than 47% of U.S. adults said they were extremely proud. Political affiliation significantly shapes responses, with 70% of Republicans saying they are extremely proud, 28% of independents, and only 14% of Democrats. Only 43% of all Americans display the U.S. flag outside their homes on national holidays or other days. Researchers noted the latest reading dropped eight points from the previous year, one of the largest single-year declines in the trend.

cards.headline: Half of Americans show middling enthusiasm for 250th anniversary of Declaration of Independence
cards.teaser: A new poll shows half of Americans are extremely or very proud of the 250th anniversary, while the other half express moderate, little or no pride.
cards.body:
Saturday brings the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, but a new poll by the Public Religion Research Institute shows many Americans have middling enthusiasm about the milestone. The PRRI survey of more than 5,000 adults found that 49% say they are extremely or very proud of the anniversary, while the other half expressed moderate (22%), little (15%), or no pride (12%). This response mirrors results from 1976, when an American National Election Studies poll found 48% of Americans were very proud of the bicentennial anniversary.

The survey revealed significant demographic differences in pride levels. Among racial groups, 58% of White Americans say they are proud of America's 250-year history, compared with 45% of multiracial Americans, 41% of Hispanic Americans, 39% of Asian American-Pacific Islanders and 22% of Black Americans. Education levels also showed disparities, with 62% of Americans without a college degree proud of the anniversary versus 51% with a college education. Age produced the largest splits, ranging from 66% of those 65 and older to just 32% of those 18 to 29 years old. Gender also differed, with 53% of men and 45% of women expressing pride in America's 250-year history.

cards.headline: Florida earns near-perfect 97.73% score on special education federal report
cards.teaser: The U.S. Department of Education awarded Florida its highest score in at least five years on the State Performance Plan for special education.
cards.body:
The U.S. Department of Education recently awarded Florida an almost perfect score of 97.73% on the State Performance Plan/Annual Performance Report for special education. This is Florida's highest score in at least five years. The report measures performance for students with disabilities from ages 3 to 21 on 18 federal indicators, including student achievement, educational environments, and dispute resolution.

Florida serves over 2.8 million students in public schools, with over 15% (448,966) identified as students with disabilities. The state has a significant history of supporting students with disabilities through services that have resulted in positive secondary transition and post-school outcomes. Florida remains committed to building on these successes to strengthen educational opportunities for all students.

cards.headline: Trump announces first-ever Republican midterm convention in Dallas for September
cards.teaser: President Donald Trump announced the Republican Party will hold its first midterm convention on Sept. 9 and 10 in Dallas, Texas.
cards.body:
President Donald Trump announced that the Republican Party will hold a midterm convention for the first time ever in Dallas, Texas on September 9 and 10. Trump called it a truly historic event and said the convention will celebrate the Great American Comeback and the incredible successes of the American people who transformed the country through the America First Agenda.

Trump outlined specific policy achievements including no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, no tax on Social Security, stronger borders, safest ever communities, lower costs and real affordability, more jobs, and American energy dominance. He noted that oil prices are dropping sharply even as the administration denuclearizes Iran. The event will feature hardworking Americans, innovators, entrepreneurs, manufacturers, first responders, and job creators who are powering the nation's Golden Age. Trump promised lots of great entertainment and described it as a rally like none other, stating that as America's 250th birthday approaches, Dallas will take center stage to celebrate the nation, its achievements, and its bright future.

cards.teaser: Volunteers in Medicine in Martin County is seeing more patients after enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies expired at the start of this year, leaving many low-income residents without health insurance.

Bromberg said the clinic has capacity for additional patients.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County residents on Franwood Drive hit with thousands in retroactive sewer fees from Delray Beach
cards.teaser: Homeowners along Franwood Drive in unincorporated Palm Beach County received notices demanding back payments for up to three years of sewer fees, with some bills totaling more than $4,000.
cards.body:
Several homeowners along Franwood Drive in an unincorporated Palm Beach County neighborhood received notices from the city of Delray Beach demanding back payments after the city completed an audit in April 2026. The bills cover up to three years of charges, along with new monthly sewer fees going forward. Candace Etzler received a bill for $3,139, while her neighbor Ruth Stephens said her total was $4,494.92. Etzler said at least a dozen homeowners in the neighborhood received similar notices. The residents are questioning how the back charges were calculated and fear their service could be disconnected if they don't pay.

The situation dates back to 1998, when nearby development disrupted septic systems and state law required residents to connect to the closest municipal sewer system. Stephens said the notices came as a surprise, stating "We didn't make a mistake; we tried to pay, but they said we didn't have to." City Commissioner Juli Casale defended the billing, saying the city's responsibility is to determine what costs were incurred and recover applicable fees to ensure public utility costs are paid by those receiving the service rather than being shifted to taxpayers. Some residents have already paid the fees or enrolled in payment plans. County Commissioner Marci Woodward said she has been in touch with the county attorney, who will be looking into the legality of the back charges and monthly payments going forward.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach woman raises funds for friend's family after earthquakes in Venezuela
cards.teaser: Carla Alvarado of West Palm Beach launched a GoFundMe campaign to support her best friend's family after two earthquakes struck Venezuela's coastal city of La Guaira, killing several relatives and destroying their home.
cards.body:
Alessandra De La Correa's family endured devastating losses when two earthquakes struck La Guaira, Venezuela last week. Her 17-year-old cousin Claudia, her grandmother, her uncle and his wife were killed in the disaster. De La Correa's parents survived, but the earthquakes destroyed their home and businesses. Her mother's children's clothing store, located inside a shopping mall, was completely destroyed. Her uncle's apartment building also collapsed moments before he entered it. De La Correa had visited Venezuela just weeks before the earthquakes to announce she is expecting a baby later this year. She spent Mother's Day with her family during that final visit, time she now cherishes with her grandmother.

Carla Alvarado, De La Correa's best friend since high school who now lives in West Palm Beach, launched a GoFundMe campaign to support the family after learning of the tragedy. The campaign aims to raise $15,000 and is spreading quickly. Alvarado said feeling powerless from abroad drove her to help. De La Correa said the support from friends and strangers has become a lifeline as her parents return daily to search the ruins of their apartment building for salvageable belongings. The family's immediate focus is obtaining donations to cover necessities like food, shelter and clothing.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz closed one year after opening in Everglades
cards.teaser: The controversial immigration detention facility that opened in the Everglades on July 1, 2025, has closed after housing roughly 1,500 detainees at a time during its peak.
cards.body:
Alligator Alcatraz, Florida's immigration detention facility in the Everglades, closed in June after operating for one year following its July 1, 2025 opening. ICE confirmed on June 16 that all detainees had been removed in preparation for hurricane season. The facility was constructed in eight days using emergency funding and no-bid contracts through the Florida Division of Emergency Management. Gov. Ron DeSantis announced that 21,000 detainees were deported through the facility. The state commandeered an old Miami-Dade County landing strip to build the facility, with President Donald Trump initially stating that FEMA would cover costs.

The facility faced immediate legal challenges on multiple fronts. The American Civil Liberties Union filed a federal lawsuit challenging detainees' access to legal counsel, citing restrictions on attorney visits without appointments and inability to make unmonitored calls. Using ICE's own data, approximately 70 percent of detainees had no criminal record, contradicting government claims that only dangerous criminals would be held there. Friends of the Everglades and the Miccosukee Tribe filed a separate federal lawsuit alleging construction violated the National Environmental Policy Act. A $608 million FEMA grant approved in October was stalled, leaving Florida taxpayers responsible for costs estimated at more than $1 billion. Both the ACLU and Friends of the Everglades lawsuits remain active.

cards.headline: West Palm Beach gets $2 million state funding for Australian Avenue flood repairs
cards.teaser: The new Florida budget includes $2 million in state funding for a drainage project along Australian Avenue from Banyan Boulevard through 45th Street, an area that floods even during light storms.
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a budget Monday that includes $2 million in state funding for drainage improvements along Australian Avenue in West Palm Beach, specifically targeting the area from Banyan Boulevard through 45th Street. State Sen. Mack Bernard said securing the funding was a major step forward after DeSantis vetoed $742,000 for the project last June. The $2 million covers only a portion of the project's estimated $65 million cost. According to Palm Beach County documents, the Australian Avenue improvements are part of a five-year road program scheduled to run through 2029.

Residents have reported that the roadway floods during even light storms. Theodore Vanriel, who lives near the corridor, said he has been riding his bike through flooded streets since he was a child. Marion Hawkins, who lives near the roadway, calls it "Lake Australian Avenue" because water comes all the way up to her driveway and yard and leaves debris scattered across properties after storms. Palm Beach County Public Works Director and Engineer David Ricks presented plans for improvements three years ago. The proposal included creating a larger median and expanding road and shoulder areas to make room for larger underground drainage pipes designed to reduce flooding.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound's Salty Pelican Fish Shack featured in restaurant review
cards.teaser: The Salty Pelican Fish Shack in Hobe Sound received a restaurant review highlighting the Martin County dining option.
cards.body:
A restaurant review featured the Salty Pelican Fish Shack in Hobe Sound, spotlighting the local dining establishment. The review covered the restaurant's offerings for residents and visitors in the Martin County area.

The Salty Pelican Fish Shack is located in Hobe Sound and serves seafood to customers. The review provides information for those looking for dining options in the area.
